newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Illegal immigrants find themselves in french limbo.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Illegal immigrants find themselves in french limbo.

text.p: One day, Jeanne Tchaleu took her three-year-old daughter for a walk in a Paris suburb.
When she came back the locks on the door of her apartment had been changed.
She was two months in arrears and does not have the papers to remain legally in France so the landlord did not bother going through the normal procedures in evicting her.
"I found myself in the street, on a Saturday, with a child who had wet herself, who was crying because she was hungry and in an area I didn't know," said the 31-year-old Cameroonian immigrant.

Jeanne has been in France nine years. Her daughter was born here but her mother has only a temporary residence permit which expires soon though she went on a hunger strike last year in a desperate bid to win legal status.

Before the strike, she was unknown to the authorities, an illegal immigrant without any right to live in France. After the strike, the authorities gave her a three-month residence permit, which means she can be expelled as soon as it expires.
LAWS ON IMMIGRANTS TO BE TIGHTENED
Ask what her life is like and Jeanne will speak of repeated humiliations -- and silence.
"You have to hide. People must not know that you have no papers because they could turn you in and you would find yourself behind bars."
It looks like there is no respite ahead for Jeanne, who is just one of France's estimated one million illegal immigrants.
Interior Minister Jean Louis Debre wants to crack down on the "sans-papiers" - so-called because they have no papers.
A new bill, passed by the National Assembly in December, will tighten the existing laws even further. It is due to pass the Senate in early February.
Two of the most controversial clauses would bar illegal immigrants from getting papers under any circumstance and would also restrict people's freedom to put up an illegal immigrant in their home.
PLIGHT OF "SANS PAPIERS" HITS HEADLINES

The government's hardline approach echoes elements of the policies of the far-right National Front, whose anti-immigration rhetoric helped it win 15 percent of the vote in the last presidential elections in 1995.
Though the get-tough attitude has won applause from some in gloom-ridden France where unemployment is a record 12.7 percent, it has also been a source of international embarrassment.

The case of the sans-papiers leapt on to the front pages of newspapers worldwide last August when police stormed the Saint Bernard church in the heart of Paris where hundreds of Africans had taken refuge.
Ten of them were on hunger strike to demand residency papers and the raid came on their 50th day.

The pictures of helmeted riot police smashing their way with axes into the church and dragging out men, women and children sparked outrage in France and drove thousands of protesters into the streets demanding the legalisation of the sans-papiers.
ANTI-RACIST GROUP CALLS FOR REVIEW OF LAWS
The problem is that many sans-papiers in France find themselves in a bizarre legal limbo.
The laws were last tightened in 1993 under the then-Interior Minister Charles Pasqua. Many immigrants who would have been entitled to papers before, now were not. But neither could they be expelled.
In the shadow-world of the sans-papiers, this means a constant shuttling between the police, who arrest you for not having papers, and the courts which free you because you cannot be expelled.

"We need to redo all the legislation and to see that the laws cannot be allowed to restrict fundamental rights, like the right to live in a family, the right to residency, the right to refuge," says Maloud Aounit, the secretary-general for MRAP, the Paris-based Movement against Racism.
The plight of many of those who had been in the Saint Bernard church illustrates the ambiguity. Most of them were allowed to stay when magistrates thwarted orders to expel them.
Under the new bill, the magistrates would no longer be able to do this. The sans-papiers are already mobilising against it.
In a chilly hall outside Paris, the Haute Seine collective gather twice a week to plan strategy and offer advice to those who are trying to get their cases cleared by the administration.
Children play tag as the adults talk of campaigns, support and above all solidarity.
IMMIGRANT PARENTS FIGHT FOR CHILDREN'S RIGHTS
For many parents, like Jeanne Tchaleu, the children are the reason for continuing the fight.
"As a single woman I could continue to live in the shadows, but not with a daughter, a little girl who has the right to a good education, and the right to live with me."

Lamia Bouselmi is Tunisian and has a young son. He was born in France and his father is Egyptian. No one can agree what he is. "My son now finds himself without a nationality. He has no country. Even France does not want him," she said.
Lamia, Jeanne and their friend Nadia Malhoul all went on hunger strike for 23 days last year to draw attention to the plight of the sans-papiers.
And they have little time for any suggestion that perhaps it would be easier for them if they just went home.
"I will stay until the end. I will fight until the end. That's why I went on hunger strike. And it's only the beginning of the fight," says Lamia.

For Nadia, who is Algerian and married with three children in France, going home is not an option. "There is a war in Algeria. I would like to be at home with my family. If one day my country was really at peace, I would not be here."
